How a component ships today

Figma shows how it looks. Not how it works.

figma filelayout, colour, type, variants
props?can be tricky in Figma controls
behaviour?hold, keys, haptics, timing
nested parts?which inner props to expose
iOS team"what props does it take?"
Android team"can I swap the icon?"
Design Review"why are these different?"

The file carries the look. What it leaves out, each team fills in alone, and differently.
The drift isn’t caught at handoff. It’s caught in design review, or by a user.

What a screenshot can’t carry

Six things get lost between platforms.

Prop semantics

Three APIs for one component

Call sites aren’t portable, and the docs fork.

State coverage

A state quietly goes missing

It exists on web, not on Android. Nobody notices until a designer opens the build.

Motion feel

Curves get eyeballed

Durations are copied; springs are re-tuned by hand and read differently.

Accessibility intent

ARIA doesn’t translate

Native semantics are reinvented per component, inconsistently.

Token bindings

One hardcoded hex

The rebrand ships broken on exactly one target.

Interaction logic

Hover has no touch twin

Each team invents a mapping, and they don’t agree.

02

Workflow

From a React component to native specs, step by step.

Where it starts

From Storybook into the tool.

Built and reviewed in Storybook. Quick to spin up, so you see right away if it’s built correctly.

Handed to ToNative by its folder. Code and styles are read; anything missing becomes a question.

The tool

Meet the reader.

  • Read-only by design. The only fields you can edit are the few that exist nowhere in the code.
  • One component, eight views: props, appearance, events, motion, accessibility, what’s left to the platform, the specs.
  • Its docs are generated from the source they describe, so they can’t go stale.

Workflow at a glance

How it works, in three steps.

1

Read

What it says, and doesn’t.

Props, styles, states and logic come straight from the code. Anything missing becomes a question.

2

Map

Every value, per platform.

Roles, sizes and curves become iOS and Android terms. What a platform lacks is dropped, not faked.

3

Build

Checked, then written out.

No gaps, no nulls. Then one spec file each for iOS and Android.

Lesson 1 · from Read

Behaviour ships as code, not as a guess.

You hold +, then slide your finger off. Does it keep counting?

A design note

“hold to repeat”

?

It doesn’t say. Each team guesses.

The code

onPointerLeave: stopHold

Stops.

The tool hands every team this exact line.

Step 1 · Read

Ask what it doesn’t say.

cc validate counteroutput
Counter v1.0.0  3 errors · 1 warning · 14 tokens
  !  No description.                  description
  ✗  No variant axis defined.         props.variant
  ✗  No size axis defined.            props.size
  ✗  No accessibility role declared.  a11y.role

  Open design questions
  Answer these with the designer and the iOS/Android leads.
   1. What is this component for, in one sentence?
   2. What visual variants does this component have?
   3. What sizes does this component come in?
   4. What is this, to a screen reader?
  • 53
    rules check the contract against what the component states.
  • Notes, not failuresOnly the closure check can block a build.
  • Gaps become questionsFor the designer and the platform leads, not for each team to guess.

Lesson 2 · from Read

“A spec that looks complete and is wrong is worse than one that is honestly incomplete.”

So the tool never fills a gap with a plausible value. A gap in the design stays a gap in the output: named, and visible.

Step 3 · Build

Check it’s complete. Then write it.

Closure check

  • Every row has the same fields
  • No value is null or empty
  • Rows = variants × sizes × states
  • Strict by default: an incomplete spec isn’t written

Lesson 3 · from Build

The output is data, not source.

It used to emit Swift and Kotlin. That forced SwiftUI and Compose on teams who might use neither.

Counter.swift
Counter.kt
↓ now
ios.json
android.json
Genuinely platformMerely framework
44pt against 48dpCGFloat vs Dp
a button trait against a Button roleimport SwiftUI
action against onClickColor, Font.Weight

Platform-specific. Framework-agnostic. Each team builds it in the stack it already has.

Case study · Counter

A small stepper. A lot of decisions.

  • holdRepeats every 150ms while pressed
  • keysArrows step; Page Up/Down step 10×; Home/End jump to the bounds
  • popValue scales 1 → 1.1 for 100ms. Under reduced motion, effectively instant
  • at a boundButton gets aria-disabled, not disabled, so it stays focusable
